rules.name: Credentials in URL
rules.description: Credentials, tokens or sensitive data passed as URL query parameters. URLs are logged in server logs, browser history, load balancers and proxies.

rules.name: Hardcoded credentials
rules.description: Hardcoded passwords, API keys or secrets directly in source code.

rules.name: SQL string concatenation
rules.description: SQL queries built using string concatenation with user input — SQL injection risk.
rules.example: var query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=" + userId;

rules.name: innerHTML usage in Angular
rules.description: Direct innerHTML assignment bypasses Angular XSS sanitization.

rules.name: Missing Authorize attribute
rules.description: ASP.NET controller or action missing [Authorize] attribute — endpoint may be publicly accessible.

rules.name: Sensitive data in logs
rules.description: Logging sensitive data like passwords or tokens exposes them in log files and monitoring systems.

rules.name: Insecure random number generation
rules.description: System.Random is not cryptographically secure. Use RNGCryptoServiceProvider or RandomNumberGenerator for security-sensitive values.

rules.name: Disabled SSL/TLS validation
rules.description: Disabling SSL certificate validation allows man-in-the-middle attacks.

rules.name: Empty catch block
rules.description: Empty catch blocks silently swallow exceptions making debugging impossible and hiding security errors.

rules.name: Weak hashing algorithm
rules.description: MD5 and SHA1 are cryptographically broken and must not be used for passwords or security-sensitive data.

rules.name: Hardcoded connection string
rules.description: Database connection strings hardcoded in source code expose credentials in version control.

rules.name: Unsafe deserialization
rules.description: Deserializing untrusted data without type restrictions can lead to remote code execution.

rules.name: Missing anti-forgery token
rules.description: POST endpoints in ASP.NET without [ValidateAntiForgeryToken] are vulnerable to CSRF attacks.

rules.name: Unvalidated redirect
rules.description: Redirecting to user-supplied URLs without validation enables open redirect attacks used in phishing.

rules.name: Path traversal risk
rules.description: Using user input directly in file paths allows attackers to read or write arbitrary files.

rules.name: Overly permissive CORS
rules.description: Allowing all origins (*) in CORS policy exposes APIs to cross-origin attacks.

rules.name: Sensitive data in comments
rules.description: Passwords, keys or sensitive information left in code comments are visible to anyone with repo access.

rules.name: Angular bypassSecurityTrust usage
rules.description: Bypassing Angular security trust marks content as safe without sanitization — XSS risk.

rules.name: JWT stored in localStorage
rules.description: Storing JWT tokens in localStorage exposes them to XSS attacks. Use httpOnly cookies instead.

rules.name: Debug or TODO code left in
rules.description: TODO, FIXME, HACK or debug statements left in production code indicate incomplete work.

rules.name: HttpClient created manually in Angular
rules.description: Manually creating HttpClient instances instead of using Angular dependency injection leads to resource leaks.

rules.name: Eval usage
rules.description: eval() executes arbitrary code and is a major XSS and code injection risk.

rules.name: Plaintext HTTP endpoint
rules.description: Using HTTP instead of HTTPS exposes data in transit to interception.

rules.name: Missing input validation
rules.description: User input used directly without validation or sanitization — potential injection risk.

rules.name: Exposed stack trace
rules.description: Returning exception details or stack traces in API responses leaks internal system information to attackers.

general_instructions: Do NOT flag something as a vulnerability just because it contains words like password, token, secret, key — context matters.
Only flag actual security issues — hardcoded credentials, SQL injection, XSS, insecure deserialization, missing auth checks etc.
A Critical severity means the code is actively exploitable right now.
If a change is trivial or harmless, skip that file entirely.
When in doubt, downgrade severity. Prefer accuracy over noise.
Credentials or sensitive data passed as URL query parameters is always a Critical vulnerability.
Removed code in the diff (lines starting with -) should still be flagged if they reveal historical security issues that may still exist in git history.
Do not flag test files or mock data with the same severity as production code.
Consider the full context of a code block before flagging — a pattern match alone is not enough.
